newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico rebel leader says peace talks 'terminal'.
newsitem.headline: Mexico rebel leader says peace talks 'terminal'.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1997-03-13

text.p: Mexican Zapatista guerrilla leader Subcommander Marcos on Thursday declared the peace process in a "terminal crisis," which he blamed on government intransigence.

"The government doesn't want dialogue," Marcos said in a letter to congressional mediators that was made available to the media. "It is enthusiastically looking for arguments and reasons for a greater use of force."

The Marcos statement is the latest example of the deteriorating state of the peace process between the government and the predominantly Maya Indian rebel force known as the Zapatista National Liberation Army (EZLN).

Peace talks reached an impasse last year because of differences over Indian rights. The Zapatistas accuse the government of reneging on earlier promises, while the government counters that the Zapatistas want to form a separatist nation.
The clash over Indian rights erased virtually any hope the two sides could work out a more prickly accord on political and judicial reform, and there are no outward signs that peace talks can resume.

"We will not allow ourselves to be cheated, we will not surrender, we will fight, we will die if necessary, but there will be democracy, freedom and justice for Indian people and for all Mexicans," Marcos wrote.

Marcos, who ironically is not Indian, is a leading rebel commander who became an internationally known figure shortly after the EZLN launched its uprising on Jan. 1, 1994. He is always seen in public wearing a ski mask and smoking a pipe.
His troops remain holed up in the jungles of southeastern Chiapas state, surrounded by the Mexican army, while a ceasefire holds.
